newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania's exiled king seeks government resignation.
newsitem.headline: Albania's exiled king seeks government resignation.

text.p: The exiled pretender to Albania's throne joined the country's opposition on Tuesday to press for the government's resignation over failed pyramid savings schemes which have beggared hundreds of thousands of investors.

Leka Zogu, who lives in South Africa, called on right-wing President Sali Berisha to hold fresh elections and a referendum to enable Albania's 3.4 million people to decide whether they wanted to remain under a republic or restore the monarchy.

"I think that the only way out of this (crisis) is for the present illegitimate government to resign because the people do not trust it," Zogu said in an interview with the monarchist newspaper Atdheu.

"President Berisha should accept calls for a referendum on the form of government. People must be allowed to choose again in early parliamentary elections. No government can work without the support of the people."

Zogu was the son of Albania's last king, Zog. He fled the Balkan country with his parents in April 1939 when he was just over a day old after Italy's fascist dictator Benito Mussolini sent troops to occupy it.
Enver Hoxha's Communist regime, the most repressive in eastern Europe, took power at the end of World War Two and introduced a law, still in force, prohibiting the return of the royal family.

After Zog died in Britain in 1961, Zogu was proclaimed Leka I, King of the Albanians, and moved to Spain during the rule of dictator Francisco Franco. He was later forced to leave and settled in Johannesburg.
With Hoxha's successors removed and Berisha elected to office, Zogu attempted to visit his homeland in 1993, saying he recognised the legitimacy of republican rule.
But he was unceremoniously bundled back on to a private aircraft within 24 hours on grounds that his passport marked "Kingdom of Albania" was invalid.
Albania's two small monarchist parties have attracted minimal support, though one grouping is part of a coalition running the fiercely anti-communist northern city of Shkoder.

And it is uncertain whether Zogu, now 57, would be given the same rapturous welcome King Michael of Romania, also barred from his homeland, and Simeon of Bulgaria received if he were allowed to return home.

The bespectacled Zogu, who stands two metres tall (more than six feet) stands for the creation of a "greater Albania". That would incorporate the traditionally Albanian regions of Kosovo in Yugoslavia and Cameria (Thesprotia) in Greece.

In his newspaper interview, Zogu, said the government had been wrong to draft in the army to protect government buildings set on fire by demonstrators demanding refunds of savings lost in the pyramid schemes.
"A soldier is to defend his own nation and not the buildings and temporary interests of politicians," he said.
Berisha's government, he said, was beyond redemption and the foreign community unlikely to offer any help.
"I am convinced no state will give credits to a government which has produced such blatant corruption," he said.
